The Know-Nothing Party, officially called the American Party, was a nativist political movement of the 1850s that opposed immigration and the political influence of Roman Catholics.

The party took its name from the response members gave when questioned about its secret rituals: "I know nothing." Hence the nickname.

The Know-Nothings opposed Irish and German Catholic immigration, viewing Catholics as loyal to the Pope rather than the United States and as threats to Protestant American culture. They demanded stricter naturalization laws, longer waiting periods for citizenship, and bans on foreign-born citizens holding office.

In the 1856 presidential election, Know-Nothing candidate Millard Fillmore, a former Whig president, won 21 percent of the popular vote and 8 electoral votes. This was the party's peak showing. Yet internal divisions soon weakened it. The party tried to avoid taking a stance on slavery in order to maintain both Northern and Southern support, but as the sectional crisis intensified, this balancing act became impossible.

By 1860, the party had effectively dissolved. Its anti-immigrant program was abandoned, though nativist sentiment would resurge periodically in later decades, in the Ku Klux Klan revivals and during the 1920s immigration restriction era. Fillmore would go on to become a long-serving senator from his New York home, but the Know-Nothing movement itself was a phenomenon of the antebellum era and the party realignment that preceded the Civil War.
